title: Historical Misconceptions For You to Bring Up during Family Dinner
protagonist: narrator, sent by 'the big man upstairs'; the viewer is the culprit spreading myths
want: clean up ten myths the viewer still repeats
central_question: Which ten things you believe about history are wrong? (0:21)

beats.text: Narrator gets orders from above to clear up ten myths the kid is spreading
#1 nobody was burned at Salem; the real death (a man pressed under stones) is better than the myth
#2-3 the fat Buddha is a different figure, and Buddha was just a man (a shirt gag gets sadder each time) (inner BUT)
#4 the vomitorium was only an exit (inner BUT)
#5 the cherry-tree story is fake, and makes no sense anyway (skit) (inner BUT)
#6 pyramid builders were paid workers who got better perks than space-station crews (inner BUT)
#7 the Great Wall is not visible from space (guitar-pick analogy) (inner BUT)
#8 dictators did not build the roads or fix the trains, so you have nothing left to like about them (inner BUT)
#9 iron maidens were invented by 1800s showmen (skit) (inner BUT)
#10 Einstein never failed maths; the myth comforts slackers (skit) (inner BUT)
We all have a lot to learn, which bridges into the sponsor

loops.q: what are the ten myths
who was 'squished to death' and how
was he a witch? (left open on purpose)
how sad can the Buddha shirt get (runner)
how small is the wall from space
was the dictator at least efficient
where did iron maidens come from
why does the Einstein myth exist

turns: 0:29 the real Salem death beats the myth
3:03 the dictator credit gets taken away
ending: Moral: everyone has more to learn, which leads into the sponsor. No callback to the 'big man upstairs' frame.

title: Tarrare, the Hungriest Man in History
want: to satisfy an endless hunger, and later to be cured of it
central_question: What happens to someone whose body forces him to eat like a competitive eater for life? (0:15)

beats.text: Born poor; eats a quarter of a cow a day as a teen
You'd expect him obese, but he weighs about 100 lb, with a giant mouth, a skin flap and a stench
His family throws him out
He begs and steals, then becomes a street performer who eats anything for crowds
A blockage lands him in hospital on laxatives (the narrator refuses to draw what happens next)
He joins the army looking for purpose, but quadruple rations still aren't enough
Exhausted, he goes to a military hospital, where doctors test him: a feast for 15, a live eel, a cat
Scientific verdict: a demon
The army turns the curse into a weapon: he swallows a box and passes it, so he becomes a spy
He speaks no German and eats garbage in public, so he is caught
After a beating he confesses and is chained to a latrine for 30 hours, but the note was worthless
Back at the hospital he begs for a cure, but nothing works, and he escalates to stray dogs, blood and corpses
A toddler goes missing and he is expelled
He returns years later with TB and dies; the autopsy shows a body built around food
Anti-moral: some stories have no point

loops.q: what becomes of a man cursed with endless hunger
is he obese? (no)
what happened after the laxatives (refused on purpose)
was the emptiness a lack of purpose? (no)
what experiments will the doctors run
can he swallow and deliver a box
will the spy mission work
what was the secret document
can he be cured
where did the missing child go
what was inside him

turns: 2:27 the search for purpose fails at once
3:42 the curse becomes a military asset
ending: Death and an autopsy picture (a pie chart: 90% food). Then an anti-moral: no lesson here, just sad and gross.

title: Why It Sucked to Be a Pirate
protagonist: little Jimmy, then 'you' as a would-be pirate
want: the swashbuckling life from the movies
central_question: Would it be fun to be a pirate? (0:08; the thesis 'no' comes at 0:14, and the question becomes 'how bad, and is any part good?')

beats.text: Jimmy likes the pirate movies and thinks piracy would be fun
You could not be more wrong
First the food: salted meat as tough as shoe leather
Hardtack full of weevils; the crew ate it in the dark (vegan-pirate skit)
Crowding: a second-person night below deck in the dark, wet and smelly
Bad food and cramped bunks breed disease: scurvy stage by stage
One upside: everyone's an alcoholic (a fake relief)
After all that misery, surely the battles are thrilling?
Most ships surrendered, and real fights were gory, not duels
Jack Sparrow wouldn't last a second (prison skit)
Don't become a pirate

loops.q: why exactly would it suck
how do you eat bug-filled bread
what is that wet / furry thing in the dark
is the moaning guy dying
how does scurvy progress
at least the battles are fun, right?
would the movie hero survive

turns: 3:23 the last hope (combat) is worse than the rest
4:13 the movie hero from the hook would die
ending: A callback to the opening's movie fantasy (Jack Sparrow dies in a skit), then one line of advice. Closes the loop the hook opened.

title: The Presidential Assassination Nobody Talks About
engine: real-person discovery (rise-and-fall, a failed quest for recognition)
want: approval and a prestigious appointment he believes he is owed (fame)
central_question: How does a 'pretty silly guy' end up killing a president that nobody remembers? (0:10-0:36)

beats.text: Childhood: his mother dies and his father is harsh and religious, so he craves approval and can't take criticism
He fails the university entrance exam
He joins a utopian commune (long digression on its strange rules)
Everyone there hates him, he gets none of the free love, and they nickname him 'get out'
He leaves; his newspaper and his lawsuit both fail
He becomes a lawyer, really a debt collector, and then a con man
His clients send a debt collector after him, so he flees
He goes into politics, giving a speech he thinks will earn him a ministry
Nobody hears it and the candidate loses in a landslide
Divorce scheme, a plagiarised holy book, moving at night to dodge debts
His candidate loses the nomination to Garfield, so he swaps the names in his speech
Garfield wins and he believes he is owed a consulship
Nothing comes; he writes letters, stalks, and is finally screamed at to go away
He decides God wants Garfield removed, picks the gun that will look good in a museum, and shoots him
Garfield lingers 11 weeks; his doctors probably killed him
The murder charge is exactly what Guiteau wanted: national fame at last
He turns his trial into a show and is hanged reciting a poem
Mock moral: you can't get what you want, unless it's being hated (bridges into the sponsor)

loops.q: who is the second forgotten assassin (dropped, a series tease)
how does a silly guy become an assassin
what made this commune special
how can selective breeding coexist with free love
will he get any free love
will the speech win him a ministry
how do you divorce without grounds
will he get his consulship
why the fancy gun (he wants fame), paid off at the trial
could Garfield have survived

turns: 7:06 his candidate loses, so he just swaps the name
9:22 punishment = the fame he always wanted
ending: The hanging, a crowd skit ('I want my money back'), and a mock moral that pays off his want (approval comes only as hatred), which bridges into the sponsor. Note: 6:06-7:06 is missing from the captions.

title: Obscure Obsolete Inventions
protagonist: none fixed; each item gets a hypothetical buyer with a problem ('you')
want: per item: solve a silly problem (stinky baby, shooting round corners, a locomotive you can't afford)
central_question: Which 'good ideas' ended up remembered as foolish, and why? (0:20)

beats.text: Premise: a good idea now is often a foolish memory later
Moonlight towers: one giant light, but dim and full of UV (inner BUT)
Baby cages for stinky babies, until society decided babies mattered more (inner BUT)
Acoustic mirrors heard planes across the Channel, but radar made them useless (inner BUT)
Looks like a torture device, but it's a beauty micrometer; women refused it (inner BUT)
A curved gun barrel (cartoon logic), but it broke and shattered bullets (inner BUT)
A revolver mousetrap
A horse-on-a-treadmill locomotive, 2-4 horsepower (inner BUT)
Smoking novelties, which bridges into the sponsor

loops.q: which inventions, and why did they flop
one big light instead of many? does it work
how do you air out a stinky baby
how do you hear planes coming
is this a torture device
can you shoot around corners
a mousetrap with more property damage?
cheap locomotive?

turns: 2:44 it worked, then radar killed it
ending: No resolution or callback; the last item turns straight into the ad.

title: Why Produce Used to Suck
engine: mystery (origin reveal: what was it before?)
protagonist: humanity as a breeder; secondary: the stranded castaways in the hook (dropped)
want: to turn useless wild plants into delicious food
central_question: Why is the 'perfect' island banana a lie, and what did our food used to be? (0:24)

beats.text: Movie trope: castaways find a perfect banana tree
The narrator stops them: those bananas are lies
Fruit exists to bribe animals into carrying seeds
Humans bred them for thousands of years into deformed treats
Bananas: wild ones are seed-packed, modern ones are sterile
Watermelon: a bitter tennis ball 5,000 years ago; a painting shows the change
You hate cabbage but like broccoli? They're the same species (inner BUT)
Eggplant: once a green berry
Digression: Grimace used to be evil
Corn's ancestor isn't baby corn, it's garbage with 5-12 rock-hard kernels (inner BUT)
Human effort transforms things, which bridges into the sponsor

loops.q: why are the bananas 'made of lies'
why does fruit exist at all
what did bananas used to look like
what if you plant a modern banana
how old and how different is watermelon
which of these vegetables do you like
why is it called an eggplant
what did old corn look like
will the castaways survive (frame dropped)

turns: 0:24 the rescue fruit is a lie
ending: A generic 'humans can do amazing things' line into the sponsor. The desert-island frame is never called back.

title: Casually Explained: Being Healthy
engine: other:myth-bust list, then a toolkit applied
protagonist: 'you' (and the narrator), against internet nutrition advice
want: to know what actually makes you healthy
central_question: Nobody explains WHY foods are healthy, so what actually works? (0:00; core answer at 2:24)

beats.text: Premise: we're told what's healthy but never why
'Superfood' just means 'grows in nature', and half our advice is Pinterest
Myth: detox foods are really just laxatives
Myth: more antioxidants are always better (the motor-oil analogy) (inner BUT)
Myth: never skip breakfast (intermittent-fasting joke) (inner BUT)
Diet tribes and their smugness
The real rule: calories in vs calories out
The three macronutrients, plus alcohol as a bonus
With those basics, judge every popular diet: each has pros and cons
Gym myths: 'toning' and 'getting too big' (inner BUT)
Strength plus cardio; walking covers the basics; the gym as a lifestyle punchline

loops.q: why is anything healthy
do detox foods work
are more antioxidants better
must you eat breakfast
which diet is right
why do some people say calorie counting is false
can you 'tone'
will lifting make you too big

ending: Practical summary with a joke on the gym lifestyle. No callback.

title: Casually Explained: The English Language
engine: versus/conflict (English speakers vs everyone learning English)
protagonist: the narrator as a smug native English speaker
want: to feel good about his language (the 'hardest language' claim)
central_question: Is English really one of the hardest languages? (0:25)

beats.text: The world learns English; English speakers don't bother learning anything
Map: Nordics speak 2.5 languages, the UK 1.6, America is stuck on kilometres
The comforting claim 'English is hardest' is false; difficulty depends on your mother tongue
English still has quirks both ways: no gendered nouns (easy)
But 'the' and the th sound torture learners (a revenge skit for his French failures)
Hard words for everyone; the viewers say them together
Spelling and sound don't match (though / tough / cough)
Dialects: the American, British and Australian versions of one sentence
Every accent has pros and cons; his bland accent can't rap but can trigger voice assistants
Sting: he uses it to subscribe your phone

loops.q: is English hardest
does English have quirks that make it easier or harder
how does he get revenge for French
which words are hard even for natives
how do the dialects differ
what is his accent good for

turns: 4:37 his useless accent has one use
ending: An interactive sting (a voice-assistant 'subscribe' prank) that pays off the 'every accent has an advantage' line.

title: Casually Explained: Reddit
engine: other:identity ladder (newcomer guide that ends in assimilation)
want: to fit in and earn karma
central_question: How does Reddit work and how do you fit in? (0:08), which turns into 'what do I get for all my karma?' (5:38)

beats.text: Narrator's credentials: ten years, no self-control
A guide for confused newcomers
Navigation: the search bar is decoration
Subreddits as filters
Lurking teaches you wrong facts, so posting earns karma: the goal is set
Karma route 1, comments: the formula of every thread
Karma route 2, posts: know your audience, a long subreddit catalogue
After years of this, what can you do with your karma?
Nothing; and you can't leave: muscle memory reopens the app
You've been assimilated: a checklist of the stereotype you've become
Last image: world disaster, you whisper the site's infamous slogan

loops.q: how do you fit in
how do you navigate
what is karma
how to get karma from comments
how to get karma from posts
what is karma for
how do you leave

turns: 5:47 the prize is worthless and the exit is locked
ending: The protagonist has become the joke: an identity checklist, then the slogan as the final line.

title: Casually Explained: Cooking
engine: other:identity ladder (the life cycle of a hobby)
want: to impress someone, then to get good, then maybe to go pro
central_question: How do you cook, and how far does it go? It becomes 'should I go pro?' (3:15)

beats.text: Motives: impress a date, or your mom is out
Step one is always watching a celebrity chef and picking a recipe far beyond you
Lesson learned, so pick something manageable; the hard part is 'serves two'
Prep: buy and lay out the ingredients, cross out the ones you lack
Sharpen the knife for the sound, not the result
Instagram the prep, wrap the smoke detector, wine as a 'coping mechanism'
Plating, amateur vs pro
Reflect on everything that went wrong, then leave the recipe one star
Next level: onion technique, a pricey knife, a cast-iron obsession, a gadget used once, then broke, then tattoos for life
Should I go pro?
The customers, and you'll eat frozen pizza at home
Other pros dream of gold medals; a chef dreams of a tyre company's approval
Sponsor opened with a 'five stars' callback

loops.q: why start cooking
what's the first step
what went wrong
how do you level up
should you go pro
what does a pro chef dream of

turns: 0:13 the first attempt is doomed by ambition
3:05 the hobby costs you your marriage and your money
3:57 the top honour comes from a tyre company
ending: A twist on the definition of success (the Michelin tyre company), then a callback inside the sponsor read.
